parakeet: In practice, hell is not treated as conquered. It's treated as fully operational. It still generates the fear that drives the altar calls, powers the evangelism, and makes leaving the faith feel like eternal self-destruction. When you look at the raw data, the reality becomes glaringly obvious. The grave in hell were triumphantly defeated in the sermon, but they were left fully intact in the cemetery and the system. Let's move on to our next claim. Jesus received all authority and yet has no recognizable authority. If the story is to be believed, Jesus rose from the dead with absolute unconditional power. In Matthew 28, he makes the ultimate power claim. All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. It's a bold proclamation. But there's a massive disconnect between that text, human history, and the reality right in front of our faces. If Jesus was handed all authority on earth, what exactly is he doing with it? Look at the global landscape. Seriously, we don't live in a world reflecting the singular authority of a benevolent Christ. We see democracies, republics, communist one party states, Islamic republics, secular states, and even corporate controlled oligarchies. We see a planet fractured by brutal ethnic, religious, and economic power struggles. If all authority belongs to Jesus, why does the earth still look like authority belongs to whoever has the biggest army, the most money, the loudest mythology, or the most weapons? And this isn't just a modern critique. This problem is baked right into the New Testament itself. If Jesus received all authority, why did his closest followers keep getting executed by competing authorities? The scriptures themselves are full of this tension. In Acts 7, Stephen is brutally stoned to death while calling out to Jesus. In Acts 12, King Herod has James, the brother of John, executed with a sword. Second Timothy explicitly warns that everyone who wants to live a godly life will be persecuted. First Peter claims that the devil is still prowling around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour. If Jesus has all the power in heaven and on earth, why does the New Testament read like his followers are constantly living under everybody else's power? Rome still had the swords, Herod still had the prisons, religious elites still had the stones, and the devil was still roaming free like nobody ever bothered to put him on a leash. The story promises a cosmic takeover, but the reality both then and now looks like business as usual.
